Spitefully
spite'ful-ly
adv. (with spite or malice; malignantly; with intent to injure)
From spiteful, from spite, a contraction of despite, from Latin despicere, to look down upon. Spite is contempt turned into action — injury done for the pleasure of doing it.

Biblical Definition

The adverb appears twice, and both times describes how messengers of God are handled. The first is in the parable of the marriage feast: “And the remnant took his servants, and entreated them spitefully, and slew them” (Mat 22:6). The servants brought an invitation to a wedding; the response was torture and murder. Nothing in the errand provoked it, which is the point — spite does not require a cause, only an occasion. The second is the Lord's own prediction of His passion: “For he shall be delivered unto the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on” (Luk 18:32). Christ names the treatment before He receives it, and the list is not of legal penalties but of humiliations: mocking, spite, spitting. These add nothing to the execution; they exist purely to degrade. So Scripture puts the word twice where the gospel is being carried and twice where it is answered with malice, and then commands the opposite from those who suffer it: “pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you” (Mat 5:44), and “not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing” (1Pe 3:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines spitefully as with spite; malignantly; with desire to vex, annoy or injure; malignly.

SPI'TEFULLY, adv.

With spite; malignantly; with desire to vex, annoy or injure; malignly.

They took his servants and entreated them spitefully. Matt. 22.

Spite is a contraction of despite, from the Latin despicere, to look down upon or despise.

It denotes a malignant desire of injuring another, without provocation proportioned to the act.

Key Scripture

Matthew 22:6 — "And the remnant took his servants, and entreated them spitefully, and slew them."

Luke 18:32 — "For he shall be delivered unto the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on:"

Matthew 5:44 — "But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;"

1 Peter 3:9 — "Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing."

Modern Corruption

Spite is the one motive the modern account of human nature cannot accommodate, so it is renamed as grievance and thereby justified.

expand to see more

Every secular anthropology assumes men act from interest — they seek advantage, security, or relief. Spite breaks the model, because spite will pay to hurt. Matthew 22:6 describes men who gained absolutely nothing by torturing a wedding messenger. The Reformed doctrine of total depravity is the only account that predicts this without embarrassment: the fallen will is not merely misinformed about its own good, it is hostile, and hostility does not need a profit motive. Where that doctrine is abandoned, spite must be re-explained as a response to injury — and so every spiteful act acquires a justifying history and becomes a grievance.

Luke 18:32 shows the same malice reaching its object. The spitting added nothing to the crucifixion; it was gratuitous, and the Son of God foretold it among the things He would receive. That is where the command in Matthew 5:44 gets its force. Praying for those who despitefully use you is not a technique for de-escalation and not an assertion that the malice is imaginary — the Lord names it plainly and then says pray. Blessing in return is possible only because a righteous Judge has the case (1Pe 2:23), which is precisely the doctrine the reviling age has lost.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hubrizo (G5195), to treat insolently, outrage; epereazo (G1908), to use despitefully; Latin despicere, to look down upon.

expand to see more

Greek hubrisan (G5195) — they outraged, treated with insolence; Matthew 22:6 and Luke 18:32, the root of English hubris.

Greek epereazonton (G1908) — those who use despitefully, who threaten and abuse; Matthew 5:44.

Greek emptusthesetai (G1716) — He shall be spat upon; Luke 18:32, a humiliation adding nothing to the sentence.

Greek loidorian anti loidorias (G3059) — railing for railing; 1 Peter 3:9, forbidden outright.

Latin despicere — to look down upon; Webster's root, contempt before it becomes injury.

Usage

"“Entreated them spitefully, and slew them” — over a wedding invitation."

"“Mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on” — foretold, and none of it added to the sentence."

"“Pray for them which despitefully use you” — named plainly, then prayed for."
